Chapter 8: The Twentieth Century—Fragmentation, Despair, and the Rise of New Ideologies
Imagine the dawn of the twentieth century—there’s this electric sense that anything’s possible. Airplanes are lifting off for the first time, radio waves are carrying voices across continents, and suddenly, the whole world feels a bit closer, a bit more connected.
But underneath all that excitement, old wounds are still there, quietly simmering. The hope that progress and reason could solve everything? That idea takes a serious hit. Two world wars erupt, the horrors of the Holocaust come to light, and the shadow of nuclear weapons hangs over everyone.
Picture a soldier coming home from the trenches. He looks around and realizes the world he left behind? It’s just gone—replaced by ruins and dreams that feel more like distant memories. Suddenly, finding meaning in life isn’t just a question, it’s a genuine struggle. Philosophers and artists start wrestling with questions that have no easy answers.
Out of all that chaos, new ideologies start to rise up, trying to fill the emptiness. Some people turn to communism, hoping it’ll create a fairer, more just world. Others are drawn to fascism, craving order and a strong sense of identity when everything else feels so uncertain. And a lot of folks, honestly, just dive into consumerism—buying more, chasing comfort, trying to distract themselves from all the noise.
Imagine a young couple, raising their kids in a city overflowing with people and confusion. They’re just trying to build something stable, something they can actually believe in. But those old foundations? They’re gone. And whatever’s replacing them doesn’t feel all that solid either.
Even the arts start to reflect this sense of fragmentation. Painters leave realism behind and explore abstraction. Writers experiment with how they tell stories, twisting form and meaning in ways that feel new—and kind of unsettling. You go to the movies, and the filmmaker’s trying to capture just how chaotic modern life really is. It leaves you thinking, searching, sometimes even a little uneasy.
In all this confusion, some voices start calling out for a return to the biblical worldview—a foundation that can offer hope and a sense of coherence. But for so many, faith now feels remote, maybe even out of reach. And that’s really the story of Western culture in the twentieth century—a story of longing and loss, of people searching for meaning in a world that just doesn’t make sense anymore.
